hook_text: Berlin, November 1884. Fourteen countries around a table. A map of Africa on the wall. Not one African in the room.
clip_script: In 1870, Africans ruled about nine tenths of their continent. Then European factories wanted rubber, palm oil and markets. Germany and Italy wanted empires. Britain took Egypt to guard the Suez Canal. Leopold of Belgium and France raced for the Congo. To avoid war with each other, the powers met in Berlin. Bismarck hosted. Fourteen countries. No Africans. They agreed: free trade on the Congo, the Congo Free State for Leopold, and one big rule. If you want land, you must really occupy it. So they rushed. By 1914, about nine tenths of Africa was under European rule. Only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed free.
visual_style: A whiteboard conference table with fourteen flags and an empty chair, a large map of Africa on the wall shading in from coasts to interior, and a counter rising from ten to ninety per cent.
pacing: Measured, with emphasis on the empty chair and the final figure.
